case.case_title: Cannosa Investments Limited v. Earnest Perera and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application 12/90, decided on 10 October 1990

clause.text: Any person detained shall be brought before a judge and cannot be held without legal order.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the detention of persons pursuant to the search warrant violated the right under Article 13(2) to be brought before a judge and not held without legal order.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that the detention was wrongful and mala fide, and that the police acted for collateral purposes without proper legal basis.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the detention was pursuant to a judicial order (search warrant) and thus lawful, and that mala fides on the part of police do not convert judicial acts into executive or administrative action violating fundamental rights.
key_facts: Search warrant issued by Magistrate without compliance with statutory preconditions.
Police executed the warrant and detained persons and property.
Petitioner alleged mala fide conduct by police and misuse of judicial process.
Court considered precedents on liability for acts done pursuant to judicial orders.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court interpreted Article 13(2) as protecting against detention without legal order and requiring prompt production before a judge. However, where detention is pursuant to a judicial order, even if obtained maliciously or on false material, it does not constitute a violation attracting relief under Article 126. The Court reaffirmed that judicial discretion and orders are immune from fundamental rights claims under Article 126.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the detention was pursuant to a judicial order, and although the Magistrate admitted inadvertent issuance of the warrant, this did not amount to executive or administrative action violating Article 13(2). The petitioner was not entitled to relief for wrongful detention under this clause.
principles_established: Detention pursuant to judicial order is not a violation of Article 13(2) even if the order was maliciously obtained.
Wrongful exercise of judicial discretion does not attract liability under Article 126.
Police officers acting under judicial orders are protected from fundamental rights claims.

outcome.holding: The application under Article 13(2) was dismissed as the detention was pursuant to a judicial order and did not violate the right to be brought before a judge or not held without legal order.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(2) was directly engaged because the petitioner challenged the legality of detention, but the Court held that detention under judicial order does not violate this clause.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court held that detention pursuant to a judicial order, even if maliciously obtained, does not attract liability under Article 126 and thus no violation of Article 13(2) occurred.
